description: We’re a Córdoba-based team of programmers at different stages: a 3rd-year CS student (C/C++, Linux, HPC), a 1st-year CS student, a high school programming student, and a final-year software technician. We’re eager to learn and build something real with NASA data. Looking for: data analysis/ML, UI/web design, GIS or remote sensing, and someone with a science background (physics, biology, earth science). All levels welcome!
summary:
Terra Analog Index is an open web app that searches all of Earth's land for the best analogs of the lunar south pole and Mars's Jezero crater. We divided the planet into about 21,000 one-degree cells and measured each on terrain, temperature, water and ice, and, for Mars, dust and wind, using NASA open data (MODIS, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2) and NOAA's ETOPO elevation model, compared against LRO and MOLA mission data and Perseverance measurements. An astrobiology layer adds about 20,000 extremophile records from NCBI BioSample.

Users set how much each dimension counts, explore a ranked map, and open a site card that shows where each place matches the target, where the analogy breaks down, and what Earth can never reproduce, such as reduced gravity, vacuum and radiation. The method rediscovers known analogs without being told where they are: Ross Island ranks first of 21,357 cells for the Moon, and Atacama ranks in the top 0.2% for Mars. It also surfaces candidates outside the usual list, such as the Qaidam Basin and Iran's Lut Desert.

Every system bound for the Moon or Mars is tested on Earth first. Terra Analog Index gives mission planners a transparent, reproducible way to choose where.
details:
Terra Analog Index: Project Details

What it does

Terra Analog Index is a global search engine for planetary analogs. You choose a target, either the lunar south pole (the Artemis landing region) or Jezero crater on Mars (where Perseverance is collecting samples), and the app ranks every land area on Earth by how closely it reproduces that environment. It also explains, variable by variable, where each match holds and where it breaks down.

The app has five parts:

  • Interactive world map. Every 1° cell of land (about 110 × 110 km) is colored by its total similarity to the chosen target. Known analog sites are marked, so new candidates are easy to spot.
  • Weight sliders and a live ranking. Users decide how much each dimension counts, and the ranking recalculates instantly. A team testing a drill in icy ground, a team training astronauts in rough terrain, and a team testing a life-detection instrument each get a ranking that fits their question.
  • Site cards. Selecting a cell opens a card with a radar chart of its dimensions and a side-by-side comparison of Earth's value against the target's real value for each variable. It cites the source of every number and lists the properties no place on Earth can reproduce for that target. For three finalist sites, the team also wrote cards by hand, backed by literature. Each says what is known about the site, what it could be used for (labeled as a hypothesis), where the analogy fails, and what should be checked in the field.
  • Caves and lava tubes layer. An optional layer marks caves and lava tubes already studied as Moon and Mars analogs, drawing on sources such as NASA BRAILLE, NASA SSERVI FINESSE, ESA PANGAEA-X and CHILL-ICE. These sites are important for future shelters and subsurface science, but too small to show up at 110 km resolution.
  • Method tab and data export. The Method tab explains every dataset, license, scoring rule and limitation, and shows the full validation table. Users can download the visible ranking, or the top 2,000 cells, as CSV.

How it works

1. Measuring Earth. An offline pipeline of nine steps downloads about 5.9 GB of open data. It reduces each dataset to one value per land cell for 2024:

For the biology layer, we queried NCBI BioSample for samples from extreme environments: hypersaline lakes, permafrost, hyperarid soils, acid mine drainage, hot springs, and radiation-resistant organisms. We parsed their coordinates and assigned them to cells. The result is 19,778 georeferenced records across six types of extremophile: halophiles, psychrophiles, xerophiles, acidophiles, thermophiles and radiation-resistant organisms.

2. Describing the targets. Terrain for the lunar south pole comes from the LRO LOLA polar elevation model, and terrain for Jezero comes from the Mars Global Surveyor MOLA global mosaic. Some values can't be read from a map. These come from peer-reviewed literature and are cited in the app:

  • Moon: Diviner temperatures (Williams et al., 2017) and evidence of surface ice (Li et al., 2018).
  • Jezero: temperatures, dust and wind measured by Perseverance's MEDA weather station (Rodriguez-Manfredi et al., 2023; Newman et al., 2022).

Every target value records whether it was measured or taken from literature, and where it came from.

3. Scoring. The hardest problem was that the Moon and Mars are often beyond anything on Earth. No place on Earth reaches −223 °C. A plain distance formula would rate all of Earth as equally unlike the Moon, which tells nobody anything. So each variable is scored from 0 to 1 by one of three rules, picked automatically and recorded in the output so it can be audited:

  • Similarity: used when Earth's range includes the target's value, such as slope, roughness and Jezero's wind. The score drops as a cell moves away from the target's value.
  • Directional: used when the target is beyond Earth's range, such as lunar cold or Jezero's dust. The score rewards being among the most extreme places on Earth in that direction. A 0.95 means "colder than 95% of Earth's land", not "95% like the Moon", and the card always shows the target's real value next to it.
  • Presence or absence: used for ice, depending on whether the target has surface ice.

A dimension's score is the average of its variables. The total is the weighted average of the dimensions that have data. Missing data stays visible as "no data" from the pipeline all the way to the screen and is never quietly counted as zero. A cell needs data in at least two of the three core physical dimensions to be ranked.

4. Validation. Before trusting any new candidate, we checked whether the index rediscovers analogs the scientific community already uses, without being told where they are. Each target is compared against 21,357 eligible cells.

  • Moon: Ross Island, Antarctica, ranks #1, and Concordia Station (Dome C) reaches the 93rd percentile.
  • Mars: the Atacama Desert at Yungay ranks #52 (top 0.2%), Death Valley's Ubehebe crater ranks #115, and the Licancabur and Altiplano lakes rank #127.
  • Failures: Haughton Crater misses the top 10% for the Moon (86th percentile), and the McMurdo Dry Valleys miss for Mars. Both failures are shown in the app.
  • Not counted: some analogs are chosen for things we don't measure, such as Río Tinto's acidic water chemistry. These are labeled as not covered and are not counted toward the result.

5. New candidates. Once the method passed validation, we looked at high-ranking cells that aren't known analogs. We chose three finalists that we found no literature describing as analogs of these targets:

  • Northern Ellesmere Island, Canada (Moon). This is the best cell for the lunar south pole outside Antarctica (total 0.67), and terrain and water and ice score high. It is a polar desert with continuous permafrost, and NASA is already developing a lightweight permafrost drill at Eureka, on the same island. It could serve for testing drilling and sampling in icy ground. The card is clear about where the match fails: the daily temperature range is 0.9 °C against 152 °C at the target, and the minimum is −37 °C, not −223 °C.
  • Turkestan plains, northern Afghanistan (Mars). These stony plains with loess and salt pans are swept by dust storms. Terrain (0.89) and dust and wind (0.91) are close to Jezero: dust optical depth is 0.18 against 0.45, and wind is 3.8 m/s against 4 m/s. That makes the site interesting for testing instruments and rover operations. It is far warmer than Jezero, though, and has no extremophile records, which may simply mean nobody has sampled it.
  • Chocolate Mountains and Salton Sea, California (Mars). This cell is very dry (water and ice score 0.94) and has 158 NCBI records of salt-loving and dryness-tolerant microbes from hypersaline sediment and desert soils. It is a candidate for rehearsing the search for life in salty sediments. The card also flags a practical problem: much of the mountain range is a Marine Corps bombing range closed to the public.

Benefits

  • A systematic search instead of tradition. Most analog sites in use today were chosen through decades of individual fieldwork and practical access. Terra Analog Index checks every land cell on Earth against the same criteria.
  • Explanations, not a black box. Every score breaks down into dimensions and variables, and every number links to its source. A user can see why a site ranks high and argue with it.
  • Adjustable to the mission. Different tests need different analogs, and the weights let each user ask their own question.
  • Honesty about limits. Each card lists what Earth can't reproduce: lunar gravity (1.62 m/s²) and Martian gravity (3.71 m/s²), vacuum or a thin CO₂ atmosphere, unshielded radiation, abrasive charged regolith, perchlorates and global dust storms. Users can see where a test on Earth stops being valid.
  • Fully open and reproducible. Every input is open data, the code is public, and one command rebuilds every result from the raw downloads.
  • Fast and lightweight. The processed data is 1.8 MB, and the app runs on a free cloud plan or any laptop.

Intended impact

Every system that goes to the Moon or Mars is tested on Earth first, including rovers, drills, suits, life-detection instruments, habitats and the operations plans that tie them together. Demand for good testing grounds is growing as Artemis targets the lunar south pole and Mars sample science continues.

We want Terra Analog Index to:

  1. Help mission and instrument teams find and justify test sites, including ones closer to home or more accessible than the classic locations.
  2. Diversify analog research by surfacing well-matched regions that haven't yet been described as analogs, such as northern Afghanistan. This could open fieldwork opportunities in regions and countries that rarely host it.
  3. Connect planetary science with astrobiology, by pointing life-detection teams to places where extremophiles are documented under conditions resembling the target.
  4. Teach and engage the public with a tool that makes concrete how similar, and how different, Earth is from the worlds we plan to explore.

The framework is general. Adding a new target, such as another lunar region, a Martian lava plain or an icy moon, only takes a new target profile. The planned next step is refining finalist regions to 0.5° resolution.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Language: Python 3.11+
  • Geospatial and scientific processing: xarray, rioxarray, rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, NumPy, pandas, netCDF4, pyhdf (for MODIS HDF4 files)
  • Biology data: Biopython (NCBI Entrez API)
  • Data storage: Apache Parquet via PyArrow, with JSON for target profiles and validation; Pydantic models check every file against a documented contract
  • Web app: Streamlit, with Plotly for the map, radar charts and figures
  • Testing: pytest, with 435 automated tests covering the pipeline, scoring rules, coordinate parsing, data contracts and app views
  • Build and reproducibility: GNU Make, which runs the pipeline, skips steps that are already up to date and records a manifest of every run
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub, with a ticketed workflow and shared design documents
  • Deployment: Render (free web service), redeployed automatically on every push
  • Data access: NASA Earthdata Login, NASA GES DISC, LP DAAC, NSIDC, NOAA NCEI, USGS Astrogeology, NASA PGDA and NCBI
  • Hardware: the team's own laptops. The whole pipeline was designed to run on a laptop, with no cluster or GPU.

What makes it creative

  • Directional scoring for targets beyond Earth's range. Instead of pretending Earth can match the Moon, we score how far each place goes toward it and say so plainly on every card.
  • A dimension profile instead of a single score. The challenge warns that a site can be a good geological analog and a poor thermal one. Our interface is built around showing exactly that.
  • Biology alongside physics. Most analog maps stop at geology and climate. We added a layer of documented extremophile life from about 20,000 genetic sample records, bringing a biotechnology angle to site selection.
  • Self-validation built into the product. The validation table, failures included, is part of the app, not hidden in a report.
  • Candidate cards that admit what we don't know. Every proposed use is labeled a hypothesis, every card ends with what to check in the field, and practical obstacles such as a closed military range are stated alongside the scientific match.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific honesty over impressive numbers. We report failed validations, separate measured values from literature values, and never let a directional score suggest a resemblance that doesn't exist.
  • Sampling bias in the biology data. Famous sites have more samples. We used a logarithmic scale, gave biology half weight by default, kept it out of the physical similarity score, and warn on every card that zero records may mean nobody has sampled there.
  • Scale. 1° cells average out craters, salt flats and caves. We stated this, kept caves as separate points without scores, and planned a finer-resolution follow-up.
  • Data quality at the poles. Optical snow data doesn't exist during polar night, and satellite precipitation is unreliable over Antarctica. The pipeline handles both cases explicitly and labels them. The finalist cards also flag satellite values that look doubtful, such as precipitation over the Ellesmere polar desert.
  • Which dimensions apply to each target. The Moon has no atmosphere, so dust and wind count only for Mars. Geology, mineralogy and the subsurface are out of scope, and analogs chosen for those reasons are labeled "not covered" instead of being counted as failures.
  • Practical access. A strong scientific match is not useful if nobody can work there. The finalist cards note access restrictions and whether fieldwork looks feasible.
  • Fixed time window. All Earth data is from 2024, so results can be compared. Changing the year is one setting, so the analysis can be rerun for another year.
  • Licensing and attribution. Every dataset's license and citation is listed in the app and the repository.
  • Accessibility and reliability for judges and the public. The app is free to open with no login, runs offline on any laptop, and the repository includes bundled test data and step-by-step instructions.
  • A 48-hour constraint and a team of four. We planned the scope in advance, split the work by pipeline step, set checkpoints with predefined cuts, and froze features before polishing.
